commons:153352956.summary: On a page blazing with bands of yellow and orange, the white Lamb stands on a stylised Mount Zion, a mound of interlocking arches, bearing a tall cross. Around him rows of haloed figures raise stringed instruments in praise, while above a register of seated figures with books flanks winged heavenly beings. Painted by Maius for a copy of Beatus of Liébana's Commentary on the Apocalypse, the miniature turns Revelation's vision of the redeemed singing a new song before the Lamb into a jubilant pattern of colour and rhythm.
facts: The Morgan Beatus (MS M.644) was illuminated by the painter Maius (Magius), who is named in a colophon on folio 293 and a memento on folio 233.
It is one of the oldest surviving illustrated Beatus manuscripts and one of the earliest works of so-called Mozarabic art.
The Latin caption above the musicians reads, in substance, 'the Lamb standing on Mount Sion, and the hundred and forty-four thousand holding harps' (Agnus stans in monte Sion ... habentes citharas).
commons:153352956.notes: Commons gives 925–968; the Morgan Library dates the manuscript c. 945 (Wikipedia's link to the Morgan's record reads 'San Salvador de Tábara, ca. 945', while the Wikipedia text associates it with San Miguel de Escalada) — place given as León (kingdom) for that reason. The Lamb is the Apocalypse's image of Christ.

cur:monumental-oberzell-healing-blind.summary: Christ, at the left with his apostles, reaches out to touch the eyes of the blind man, who bends towards him before a towered gateway; a faded second figure at the right probably shows the man washing in the pool of Siloam. Pale blues and earthy reds predominate, framed by the illusionistic meander border characteristic of the church.
facts: The eight miracle scenes on the nave walls of St George, Oberzell, were rediscovered under later plaster in 1880; they are dated either to about 900 (late Carolingian) or, in the prevailing view, to the late 10th century (Ottonian).

Apart from Müstair, St George is the only church north of the Alps in the former Empire to preserve so complete a cycle of early medieval wall painting; the sequence runs from the entrance along the north wall to the altar and back along the south wall, culminating in the Raising of Lazarus.
In each scene Christ, larger than the other figures, stands at the left with a gesture of blessing directed into the narrative, except in two scenes where he appears twice.

cur:objects-cross-of-otto-and-mathilde.summary: A golden processional cross set with gems and pearls carries a relief figure of the crucified Christ, and below his feet a cloisonné enamel plaque shows the two donors, Abbess Mathilde and her brother Duke Otto, holding the cross between them. The jewels honour the cross as the Tree of Life and the throne of the risen Lord. It is the oldest of the great Ottonian processional crosses in Essen.
facts: It is named after Otto I, Duke of Swabia and Bavaria, and his sister Mathilde, abbess of Essen, grandchildren of Emperor Otto I; since Mathilde became abbess in 973 and Otto died in 982 it is dated between these years.
The cross is 44.5 cm high, with an oak core, and was carried on high holidays until recently.
